text: Jeffrey Edward Epstein (January 20, 1953 – August 10, 2019) was an American financier, human trafficker, child sex offender, and serial rapist. Born in Brooklyn, New York, to Pauline "Paula" Stolofsky and Seymour George Epstein, both of whom were Jewish and married in 1952, he grew up in the Sea Gate neighborhood of Coney Island with his brother Mark. Epstein was nicknamed "Bear" and Mark was called "Puggie." He attended public schools, including Public School 188 and Mark Twain Junior High School, where he earned money tutoring classmates and was described as "sweet and generous," "quiet and nerdy," and "very smart in math." In 1967, he attended the National Music Camp at Interlochen, where he showed musical talent. He graduated from Lafayette High School at age 16 after skipping two grades and studied mathematical physiology at the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University from 1971 to 1974, leaving without a degree. In 1974, at age 21, he began teaching physics and mathematics at the Dalton School on Manhattan’s Upper East Side despite lacking a teaching credential. During his time there, he allegedly showed inappropriate behavior toward underage female students, including flirting and attending parties where young people were drinking. He became acquainted with Alan Greenberg, CEO of Bear Stearns, whose daughter, Lynne Koeppel, testified that Epstein influenced a parent to advocate for him to Greenberg. After being dismissed from Dalton in June 1976 for "poor performance," Greenberg offered him a job at Bear Stearns. Epstein joined Bear Stearns in 1976 as a junior assistant, quickly advancing to become an options trader and advisor to wealthy clients such as Edgar Bronfman. In 1980, he became a limited partner and in 1981 was asked to leave for a "Reg D violation" according to his sworn testimony. He remained close to Greenberg and James Cayne, the bank’s later CEO, and was a client until Bear Stearns collapsed in 2008. In August 1981, Epstein founded Intercontinental Assets Group Inc. (IAG), which he described as a high-level bounty hunter helping clients recover stolen funds, including Spanish heiress Ana Obregón in 1982 after the collapse of Drysdale Government Securities. In the 1980s, Epstein traveled extensively between the U.S., Europe, and the Middle East, meeting Steven Hoffenberg through Douglas Leese and John Mitchell. He possessed an Austrian passport with a false name and residence listed as Saudi Arabia. Hoffenberg hired Epstein in 1987 as a consultant for Towers Financial Corporation, a collection agency, paying him $25,000 per month (equivalent to $69,000 in 2024). Together, they operated as corporate raiders, attempting to take over Pan American World Airways in 1987 and Emery Air Freight Corp. in 1988. In 1993, Towers Financial imploded as one of the largest Ponzi schemes in U.S. history, losing over $450 million (equivalent to $1 billion in 2024), with Hoffenberg claiming Epstein was intimately involved; Epstein left by 1989 and was never charged. In 1988, Epstein founded J. Epstein & Company to manage assets of clients with over $1 billion in net worth. His only publicly known billionaire client was Leslie Wexner, chairman and CEO of L Brands (Victoria's Secret), whom he met in 1986 through mutual acquaintances. Wexner granted Epstein full power of attorney in 1991, allowing him to manage finances, sign checks, and handle property transactions. Epstein managed Wexner’s wealth, including the construction of his yacht, the Limitless, and helped models like Stacey Williams. He also served as a global talent scout for Victoria's Secret, using his position to sexually manipulate young women. By 1995, Epstein was a director of the Wexner Foundation and Wexner Heritage Foundation and president of Wexner’s Property, which developed New Albany, Ohio. He earned millions in fees from managing Wexner’s affairs and frequently corresponded with L Brands executives. In 1996, Epstein renamed his firm to Financial Trust Company and relocated it to St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, to reduce federal income taxes by 90 percent, leveraging connections with JP Morgan banker Jes Staley. In 2002, his financial-administrative staff numbered 150 employees across three locations. In 2012, JP Morgan general counsel Stephen Cutler criticized Epstein as "not an honorable person" and claimed Epstein lied during a meeting with Staley and Cutler, citing Bill Gates as a character reference; the bank did not terminate Epstein until 2013, coinciding with Staley’s departure, after increased federal regulatory pressure. Epstein then moved his business to Deutsche Bank. According to Forbes in 2025, the majority of Epstein’s wealth between 1999 and 2018 came from $490 million in fees—$200 million from Leslie Wexner and $170 million from Leon Black—with the remaining $310 million from investment returns, totaling $600 million at death. He engaged with 75 lawyers, including Alan Dershowitz, Kenneth Starr, Roy Black, and Jay Lefkowitz. Senator Ron Wyden reported that U.S. Treasury files showed 4,725 wire transfers totaling $1.1 billion from Epstein’s accounts, with extensive financial correspondence from Russian banks linked to his sex trafficking activities. Forbes also reported that transfers from four banks—JPMorgan Chase, Deutsche Bank, Bank of New York Mellon, and Bank of America—totalled over $1.9 billion. Epstein was president of the Bermuda-incorporated company Liquid Funding Ltd. from 2000 to 2007, an early pioneer in the repo market that used commercial and investment-grade residential mortgages as underlying securities. The company was initially 40 percent owned by Bear Stearns and received AAA ratings from credit rating agencies. The flawed ratings of such securities contributed to Bear Stearns’ collapse in March 2008, triggering the 2008 financial crisis and Great Recession. In August 2006, shortly after the federal investigation began, Epstein invested $57 million in the Bear Stearns High-Grade Structured Credit Strategies Enhanced Leverage hedge fund. SEC filings show that Epstein’s Financial Trust Company controlled the votes for the fund. In 2005, police in Palm Beach, Florida, began investigating Epstein after a parent reported he had sexually abused her 14-year-old daughter. Federal officials identified 36 girls, some as young as 14, whom Epstein allegedly sexually abused. Epstein pleaded guilty and was convicted in 2008 by a Florida state court of procuring a child for prostitution and soliciting a prostitute as part of a controversial plea deal agreed by U.S. Department of Justice’s Alexander Acosta. He served nearly 13 months in custody with extensive work release. On July 6, 2019, Epstein was arrested on federal charges for sex trafficking of minors in Florida and New York. He died in his jail cell on August 10, 2019. Barbara Sampson, the New York City medical examiner, ruled his death a suicide by hanging, a conclusion disputed by forensic pathologist Michael Baden, leading to public skepticism and conspiracy theories. In July 2025, the FBI released closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage supporting the suicide ruling, but approximately two minutes and 53 seconds of the video was missing, and the footage was found to have been modified despite the FBI’s claim that it was raw. Since Epstein’s death, a judge dismissed all criminal charges on August 29, 2019. Epstein had a long-standing association with Ghislaine Maxwell, who recruited young girls for him, leading to her 2021 conviction on U.S. federal charges of sex trafficking and conspiracy for helping him procure girls, including a 14-year-old, for child sexual abuse and prostitution. Epstein made much of his fortune by providing tax and estate services to billionaires and was a renowned social networker with connections to businesspeople, royalty, politicians, and academics, including Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor (formerly Prince Andrew, Duke of York), Donald Trump, and Bill Clinton. Documents released by the House Democratic Caucus in September 2025 show he maintained connections with Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, Bill Gates, Larry Summers, and Steve Bannon, including over 20,000 pages of Epstein emails from 2011 to 2018, many of which included conversations about Trump. In 2017, a former senior White House official reported that Alexander Acosta, who handled Epstein’s case during the George W. Bush administration, told interviewers of President Donald Trump’s first transition team that Epstein “belonged to intelligence” and was “above his pay grade.” One of Epstein’s clients was Saudi Arabian businessman Adnan Khashoggi, who served as a middleman in transferring American weapons from Israel to Iran during the Iran–Contra affair in the 1980s, introduced to Epstein by Leese. Epstein also had ties to the British intelligence community through Steven Hoffenberg, who alleged in 2020 that Epstein was recruited in the 1980s by Leese to work for British intelligence and was introduced to Robert Maxwell by Hoffenberg.

Funding and other early companies used commercial mortgages and investment-grade residential mortgages bundled into complex securities as the underlying assets, rather than stocks and bonds. Liquid Funding was initially 40 percent owned by Bear Stearns. Credit rating agencies—Standard & Poor's, Fitch Ratings, and Moody's Investors Service—assigned the bundled securities a gold-plated AAA rating, enabling companies to access capital. However, the collapse of these complex securities due to inaccurate ratings led to the failure of Bear Stearns in March 2008 and triggered the 2008 financial crisis and the Great Recession. If Liquid Funding had held large amounts of such securities as collateral, it could have suffered significant losses. In August 2006, shortly after a federal investigation began, Epstein invested $57 million in the Bear Stearns High-Grade Structured Credit Strategies Enhanced Leverage hedge fund, which was controlled by his Financial Trust Company through a 10-percent share. The fund was highly leveraged, with a 17:1 ratio, meaning for every dollar invested, $17 was borrowed; a redemption request from an investor with $57 million would have removed $1 billion from the thinly traded CDO market. This triggered a repricing process and freeze in the CDO market, leading to the fund’s collapse in July 2007 and Bear Stearns’ collapse in March 2008, with investor losses exceeding $1.6 billion. By May 2007, Epstein was negotiating a plea deal for sex with minors, and in August 2007, US Attorney Alexander Acosta began direct discussions, brokered a lenient deal due to government officials’ view of Epstein as important, and reportedly secured immunity for Epstein and four co-conspirators, as well as unnamed potential co-conspirators. As part of the negotiations, Epstein provided "unspecified information" to Florida federal prosecutors and was reportedly "Unnamed investor #1" in a June 2008 criminal case against Cioffi and Tannen, two managers of the failed Bear Stearns fund. Alan Dershowitz, one of Epstein’s attorneys, stated in 2019 that he was unaware Epstein had cooperated in any prosecution. Moody's reported on April 18, 2008, that all outstanding rated liabilities of Liquid Funding were paid in full, though the fund had not yet been sold to JP Morgan as of May 1. In 2003, New York Daily News publisher Mortimer Zuckerman partnered with Epstein, advertising executive Donny Deutsch, and investor Nelson Peltz to acquire New York magazine, but Bruce Wasserstein ultimately won the bid, paying $55 million, over $10 million above the offer. In 2004, Epstein and Zuckerman committed up to $25 million to finance Radar, a celebrity and pop culture magazine founded by Maer Roshan, which folded after three print issues and became exclusively online. Between 2002 and 2005, Epstein invested $80 million in the D.B. Zwirn Special Opportunities Fund, which invested in illiquid debt securities; by November 2006, his investment had grown to $140 million, and he attempted redemption after learning of accounting irregularities, though the fund refused, citing a standard 60 to 90-day written notice requirement and a long lockup period. The fund closed in 2008, and its remaining assets, including Epstein’s investment, were transferred to Fortress Investment Group in 2009; Epstein later went to arbitration with Fortress over the redemption, with the outcome not publicly known. After his first arrest, Epstein developed an interest in the surveillance industry and maintained a close relationship with former Israeli prime minister and defense minister Ehud Barak, exchanging private emails and meeting over 30 times between 2013 and 2017. He facilitated Barak’s interactions with Peter Thiel, Sergey Belyakov, and Viktor Vekselberg, who was connected to Vladimir Putin’s circle, as documented in leaked Barak–Epstein emails, partially corroborated by The Sunday Times. Epstein leveraged this relationship to gain access to Thiel; in 2015, he invested in Reporty Homeland Security (later Carbyne), a startup led by Barak that developed emergency communication technologies, with leadership including former special forces officer Amir Elihai and former defense ministry director general Pinchas Bukhris. Epstein pitched Carbyne to Thiel-founded Valar Ventures in 2016, which declined, though partner Andrew McCormack indicated they might revisit it later; Epstein had previously invested $40 million in Valar-managed funds in 2015 and 2016. In 2018, Founders Fund, another Thiel co-founded firm, participated in Carbyne’s $15 million Series B round (non-leading role). Between 2014 and 2016, Thiel had six scheduled meetings with Epstein at his townhouse, including with Woody Allen and Kathryn Ruemmler, though there is no record of Thiel visiting Epstein’s homes or flying on his private jet. Barak and Epstein discussed meeting Vekselberg on June 6 and 8, 2014, and in April 2015, Barak asked Epstein for his opinion on Vekselberg-backed Fifth Dimension, which shut down in 2018 after being sanctioned by the US for alleged election meddling. In August 2018, Epstein told a New York Times reporter off the record that he had blackmail material on powerful people, including information about their sexual proclivities and recreational drug use. In August 2025, author Michael Wolff stated that Epstein’s email archives, seized during an FBI raid on Herbert Strauss’s home, are likely to incriminate others. In 2003, Bloomberg journalist David Bank conducted a 5-hour interview with Epstein on Little St. James, which Bank left unpublished before Epstein’s death. In 2017, Epstein spoke in over 100 hours of interviews with Michael Wolff, released in November 2024 as part of Wolff’s Fire and Fury podcast. Maria Farmer, an artist who worked for Epstein in 1996, reported that Epstein raped her to the NYPD and FBI, but the report was not pursued. In October 2007, transgender model Ava Cordero alleged abuse and filed a lawsuit, which was dismissed, with media at the time mocking her gender identity and focusing on her mental health. Virginia Giuffre was among the first to publicly reveal her identity as an accuser in 2011. In November 2004, Palm Beach police were tipped about young women visiting Epstein’s home. In March 2005, a woman reported that her 14-year-old stepdaughter was taken to Epstein’s mansion by an older girl, allegedly paid $300 (equivalent to $480 in 2024) to strip and massage Epstein, and left wearing only her underwear. Palm Beach Police launched a 13-month undercover investigation, including a home search. During the investigation, police chief Michael Reiter accused state prosecutor Barry Krischer of being too lenient and called for FBI assistance. The FBI became involved, and interviews with five alleged victims and 17 witnesses, along with a high-school transcript and items found in Epstein’s trash and home, indicated that some girls were under 18, with the youngest being 14, many under 16. A search of Epstein’s home uncovered two hidden cameras and numerous photos of girls, some of whom were interviewed. Adriana Ross, a former model from Poland, reportedly removed computer drives and electronic equipment from Epstein’s Florida mansion before the police search. A 2005 search by detective Joseph Recarey uncovered an Amazon receipt containing books on sadomasochism. A former employee stated Epstein received massages three times a day. The FBI compiled reports on 34 confirmed minors eligible for restitution (increased to 40 in the non-prosecution agreement), with Julie Brown’s 2018 Miami Herald exposés identifying 80 victims and locating about 60. Police chief Reiter stated that “This was 50-something ‘shes’ and one ‘he’—and the ‘shes’ all basically told the same story.” Allegations included that 12-year-old triplets were flown from France for Epstein’s birthday and returned the next day after being sexually abused, and that girls were recruited from Brazil, South America, the former Soviet Union, and Europe, with Jean-Luc Brunel’s “MC2” modeling agency supplying girls to Epstein, whom he actually financed. In May 2006, Palm Beach police filed a probable cause affidavit for four counts of unlawful sex with minors and one count of sexual abuse. On July 27, 2006, Epstein was arrested on state felony charges of procuring a minor for prostitution and solicitation of a prostitute, released on a $3,000 bond. State prosecutor Krischer convened a grand jury, which reviewed evidence from only two victims and returned a single charge of felony solicitation of prostitution, to which Epstein pleaded not guilty in August 2006. Epstein’s defense team included Roy Black, Gerald Lefcourt, Harvard Law professor Alan Dershowitz, former US solicitor general Ken Starr, and linguist Steven Pinker. In July 2006, the FBI began its own investigation, nicknamed "Operation Leap Year," and despite Epstein’s lawyers requesting it be ended, the federal investigation continued. In May 2007, federal prosecutor Marie Villafaña drafted a 53-page, 60-count indictment and an 82-page memo for her supervisors, including Alexander Acosta, Jeffrey Sloman, and Matthew Menchel. Acosta agreed to a plea deal, with Alan Dershowitz helping negotiate, granting immunity to Epstein and four named co-conspirators and any unnamed potential co-conspirators. The non-prosecution agreement “essentially shut down an ongoing FBI probe into whether there were more victims and other powerful people who took part in Epstein's sex crimes,” and was kept secret from victims, despite a federal law prohibiting such actions. Acosta later stated he offered the deal.

Epstein could have faced a single Florida charge of solicitation of a prostitute, but the federal investigation continued, and in May 2007, federal prosecutor Marie Villafaña drafted a 53-page, 60-count indictment and an 82-page memo for her supervisors, including Alexander Acosta, then US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jeffrey Sloman, then First Assistant US Attorney, and Matthew Menchel, then chief of the Miami criminal division. Acosta agreed to a plea deal, negotiated with Alan Dershowitz, that granted immunity from all federal criminal charges to Epstein, four named co-conspirators, and any unnamed "potential co-conspirators," effectively shutting down an ongoing FBI probe into additional victims and powerful individuals involved in Epstein's sex crimes. The Miami Herald reported that Acosta agreed to the deal despite a federal law requiring victims to be notified, and the agreement was concealed from victims, who were instead urged to have "patience." Acosta later claimed he offered the lenient deal because he was told Epstein "belonged to intelligence," was "above his pay grade," and should be "left alone." Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida state court to two felony prostitution charges, served 18 months in prison, registered as a sex offender, and paid restitution to 30 victims identified by the FBI. The plea deal was later described as a "sweetheart deal." A federal judge found that prosecutors violated victims' rights by concealing the agreement, and an internal DOJ Office of Professional Responsibility review released in November 2020 found Acosta showed "poor judgment" for granting the non-prosecution agreement (NPA) without notifying victims. In 2019, Judge Kenneth Marra ruled the Acosta NPA violated the Crime Victims' Rights Act, and an appeals court called it "a national disgrace." The terms of the NPA were revealed after Bradley Edwards, representing two of Epstein's teenaged victims, and press lawyers successfully sued to make them public. On June 30, 2008, after pleading guilty to procuring for prostitution a girl below age 18, Epstein was sentenced to 18 months in prison; he was housed in a private wing of the Palm Beach County Stockade and allowed "work release" for up to twelve hours a day, six days a week, which violated the sheriff's own policies requiring a maximum sentence of ten months and barring sex offenders from such privileges. Epstein's cell door was left unlocked, and he had access to the attorney room with a television before being moved to an unstaffed infirmary. He worked at a foundation he created, which later dissolved after his incarceration, and the sheriff's office received $128,000 from the foundation to cover additional services during work release. The office was monitored by "permit deputies" whose overtime was paid by Epstein, who required them to wear suits and check in at a "front desk" for "welcomed guests"; the guest logs were later destroyed under department "records retention" rules, though visitor logs were preserved. Epstein used his own driver to travel between jail and his office and appointments. He served nearly 13 months of his 18-month sentence before being released on July 22, 2009, and placed on one year of probation on house arrest until August 2010. His early release was due to providing information about Bear Stearns executives Ralph Cioffi and Matthew Tannin, which was scrutinized in a SDNY court case before the bank's acquisition by JPMorgan Chase. While on probation, he made numerous trips on his corporate jet to residences in Manhattan and the US Virgin Islands, and was allowed long shopping trips and walks in Palm Beach "for exercise." After a contested hearing in January 2011 and an appeal, he remained registered in New York as a "level three" (high risk of repeat offense) sex offender, a lifelong designation. The Manhattan assistant district attorney, Jennifer Gaffney, unsuccessfully argued for a reduction to "level one," and the judge chided her. Despite Epstein's lawyer claiming he had a "main" home in the US Virgin Islands, the judge confirmed he must check in with the New York Police Department every 90 days; however, the NYPD never enforced this regulation, though non-compliance is a felony. The immunity agreement and Epstein's lenient treatment sparked public dispute, with the Palm Beach police chief accusing the state of giving him preferential treatment and the Miami Herald calling the deal "the deal of a lifetime." Following Epstein's arrest in July 2019 on sex trafficking charges, Acosta resigned as Secretary of Labor effective July 19, 2019. After Epstein's accusations became public, several individuals and institutions returned donations from him, including Eliot Spitzer, Bill Richardson, and the Palm Beach Police Department; Harvard University announced it would not return any money. Charitable donations Epstein made to finance children's education were also questioned. On June 18, 2010, Epstein's former house manager, Alfredo Rodriguez, was sentenced to 18 months in prison for obstructing justice by failing to turn over and attempting to sell a journal containing records of Epstein's activities; FBI agent Christina Pryor stated the journal contained information "that would have been extremely useful in investigating and prosecuting the case, including names and contact information of material witnesses and additional victims." On July 6, 2019, prosecutors in the Southern District of New York under Geoffrey Berman charged Epstein with sex trafficking and conspiracy to traffic minors for sex, alleging "dozens" of underage girls were brought to his mansions for sexual encounters. Judge Kenneth Marra was to decide whether the Acosta NPA should still stand. Epstein requested release on bond, offering $100 million with the condition of house arrest in his New York mansion; US District Judge Richard M. Berman denied the request, stating Epstein posed a danger to the public and a serious flight risk. On August 29, 2019, 19 days after Epstein was found dead in his jail cell, Judge Berman closed the case against him, with prosecutors stating they would continue investigating potential co-conspirators. On August 23, 2019, the Paris prosecutor's office opened a preliminary investigation into Epstein, after Yael Mellul reported the international dimensions of a pedophile network involving him, criticizing the slow pace of justice. The investigation focused on rape and sexual assault of minors under and over 15, criminal association with a view to committing crimes, and association with criminals with a view to committing offenses, aiming to find crimes committed in France and elsewhere against French citizens. An associate, modeling agent Jean-Luc Brunel, was arrested during this investigation but was found dead in jail in 2022. In September 2025, the House Oversight Committee released a 2003 birthday album titled The First Fifty Years, created for Epstein's 50th birthday, containing letters and drawings from associates. One letter was attributed to Donald Trump, though Trump has denied writing or signing it and his legal team has challenged its authenticity; media coverage highlighted the release's impact on renewed attention to Epstein's political and social connections. Epstein had high self-regard and built strong social ties through skillful human relations, stating that success was not derived from hard work or background but from who one came into contact with. He retained a working-class Brooklyn accent and wore casual clothes at formal events. Epstein dated Eva Andersson-Dubin for 11 years, mostly in the 1980s, and after her marriage to Glenn Dubin in 1994, she and her husband remained friends with Epstein. Epstein met Ghislaine Maxwell, daughter of disgraced media baron Robert Maxwell, by 1991; she came to the US in 1991 to recover from her father's death and was later implicated by accusers as procuring or recruiting underage girls and served as Epstein's chief girlfriend for an extended period. Household employees testified in 2009 that Maxwell had a central role in Epstein's life, handling staff hiring, supervision, and firing starting around 1992. In 1995, Epstein renamed one of his companies the Ghislaine Corporation in Palm Beach, Florida, which was dissolved in 1998. In 2000, Maxwell moved into a 7,000-square-foot townhouse less than ten blocks from Epstein's New York mansion, purchased for $5 million by an anonymous limited liability company with an address matching J. Epstein & Co.'s office, represented by Darren Indyke, Epstein's lawyer. A photo of Epstein and Maxwell at a cabin on Queen Elizabeth II's Balmoral estate around 1999, at the invitation of then-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, was shown in court to establish their romantic relationship. In a 2003 Vanity Fair article, Epstein referred to Maxwell as "my best friend." In 2003, for a 50th birthday gift, Maxwell assembled an album of well-wishes, including a bawdy greeting from Donald Trump; in 2025, the Wall Street Journal revealed details of the album. Virginia Giuffre stated that Epstein and Maxwell sought to use her as a surrogate mother for a baby they planned to have together. Epstein's last female partner was Karyna Shuliak, with whom he maintained a relationship even while jailed in 2019; she is "one of the largest beneficiaries" of several of his financial arrangements posthumously. Shuliak is Belarusian by birth and nicknamed "the inspector" due to her jealousy and meticulous review of Epstein's agenda and contacts. Their relationship began after Epstein's release from jail in 2010 for procuring a child for prostitution. The couple had been together in Paris before his return to the US and arrest, which she witnessed. He paid for her education as a dentist, her mother's medical care, and her parents' house in Belarus. She did not believe he sounded suicidal during a 15-minute call hours before his death, which was not logged or recorded by guards, as required. Virginia Giuffre said Epstein "picked vulnerable victims," and by age 13, she was living on the streets and abused by older men; life with Epstein provided security, as he paid her, got her an apartment, and took her to New Mexico, London, Paris, Tangiers, and his island. A woman testified in a lawsuit that Epstein employed her to procure underage girls, including at the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and she witnessed a rape by Epstein. Anouska De Georgiou, who said "Jeffrey thought that we were disposable," came to Epstein through modeling. Chauntae Davies and Rachel Benavidez came via massage services. Epstein manipulated Benavidez during a two-year stay at Zorro Ranch, expelling her when she refused to sign a non-disclosure agreement. Benavidez said: "He provided me with promises of continuing education and a clientele that's a world-class clientele. And that's kind of how he lured his tentacles into me." Ruslana Korshunova, 18 when she boarded Epstein's jet in June 2006, committed suicide by jumping from her apartment balcony at age 20. Attorney Brad Edwards, representing over 200 victims, noted that while Epstein sexually abused all these women and girls, only a small percentage were sent to be abused by other men, who were also a select few. Epstein was a longtime friend of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Tom Barrack and attended parties with or frequented many prominent people, including Harvey Weinstein, David Copperfield, Bill Clinton, George Stephanopoulos, Mark Zuckerberg, Reid Hoffman, Elon Musk, Donald Trump, Noam Chomsky, Katie Couric, Woody Allen, Jeff Bezos, Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Lewis Ranieri, Ronald Perelman, Tom Pritzker, Naomi Campbell, and Stephen Hawking. Two printed phone directories, commonly known as the "black books," included Rupert Murdoch, Michael Bloomberg, Andrew Cuomo, John Kerry, Richard Branson, Alec Baldwin, David Koch, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak, British Prime Minister Tony Blair, and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Epstein was involved with Sarah Ferguson, and Maxwell claimed he bailed her out of financial difficulties; however, their relationship became hostile by 2011. Epstein was seen at least once talking with Princess Diana.

Bill Clinton, George Stephanopoulos, Mark Zuckerberg, Reid Hoffman, Elon Musk, Donald Trump, Noam Chomsky, Katie Couric, Woody Allen, Jeff Bezos, Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Lewis Ranieri, Ronald Perelman, Tom Pritzker, Naomi Campbell, and Stephen Hawking were among the individuals associated with Jeffrey Epstein. Two printed phone directories, known as the "black books," listed Epstein's contacts, including Rupert Murdoch, Michael Bloomberg, Andrew Cuomo, John Kerry, Richard Branson, Alec Baldwin, David Koch, and Michael Jackson, as well as Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak, British prime minister Tony Blair, and Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman. Epstein had a relationship with Sarah Ferguson, which became hostile by 2011, and he negotiated a 1993 divorce settlement for Lynn Forester before her marriage to Evelyn de Rothschild; Lady de Rothschild introduced Epstein to Alan Dershowitz, with whom he had known since at least 1997, a connection revealed by flight logs in 2015. Dershowitz stated that outside of his immediate family, he only shared manuscripts with Epstein before publication. Epstein took Bill Clinton, Kevin Spacey, and Chris Tucker on a trip aboard his Boeing 727 jet. Clinton and Trump claimed they never visited Little Saint James, an island Epstein owned since 1998, until his death; however, a 2017 Freedom of Information Act request found no evidence of Clinton’s visits, and Maxwell revealed in August 2025 that Clinton, who ceased contact with Epstein in 2003, was connected to him through her, with Clinton appearing on Epstein’s flight logs at least 11 times with Sarah Kellen between 2002 and 2003. In 2014, Epstein asked Michael Wolff, an acquaintance, to write his biography; Wolff advised him on press relations, recommending not to return calls or issue "no comment," which Epstein rejected, leading to profiles in 2002 by New York Magazine and 2003 by Vanity Fair. Wolff met Epstein at a party with Malcolm Gladwell, Steven Pinker, John Brockman, and David Rockwell, where Epstein asked Rockwell to critique his architectural plans for Little St. James, an event possibly occurring in 2002 when Geraldine Laybourne was logged as a passenger between JFK and MRY. Wolff noted TED conferences served as hunting grounds for Epstein to meet influential personalities. After his 2008 incarceration, Epstein was shunned by some acquaintances; Hollywood hostess Peggy Siegal helped facilitate his return to elite circles through dinner parties at Herbert Straus house and Oscar events, stating Epstein assured her he had changed his ways. USVI attorney-general Denise George alleged in a 2020 lawsuit that Epstein raped girls on his island as young as 11. Anne Hearst said that if Siegal personally promoted Epstein as a friend, one would end up at the right hand of God; after Epstein’s release, Siegal arranged a screening of Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps in a Southampton NY mansion where he met Leon Black, Wilbur Ross, and Rudy Giuliani. Siegal invited Katie Couric, George Stephanopoulos, Charlie Rose, Chelsea Handler, Woody Allen, and Soon-Yi Previn to a 2011 dinner organized by Epstein for Prince Andrew, with Stephanopoulos now calling it a mistake. Since Epstein’s death, Siegal has been shunned by several in the film industry as one of Epstein’s tools. Brockman did not end his friendship with Epstein after the conviction; his literary dinners, often held during TED events, were funded by Epstein as documented in tax filings, allowing Epstein to mingle with scientists, startup icons, and tech billionaires. From the 1980s to the mid-2000s, Epstein frequently socialized with Donald Trump, who described him as a "terrific guy" and noted he enjoyed beautiful women, many of whom were young. In 2002, Trump remarked that he had known Jeff for fifteen years and that they were like "nightlife musketeers." In 2019, Trump said he had not been a fan of Epstein and had not spoken to him in about 15 years, though a 1992 video showed them partying together at Mar-a-Lago. A known acquaintance noted they were "tight" and each other’s "wingmen." In 2004, they became embroiled in a bidding war for a $40 million mansion, Maison de L'Amitié, in Palm Beach, which Trump won for $41 million and later sold for $95 million to Dmitry Rybolovlev—this was the last recorded interaction between them. By 2007, Trump reportedly banned Epstein from his Mar-a-Lago club for unseemly pursuit of young girls, a claim included in court documents by attorney Bradley Edwards, though Edwards later said it was a rumor he could not confirm. Epstein told Wolff in 2017 that he was Donald’s closest friend for ten years, and Wolff noted that after Trump’s election, Epstein feared Trump due to mutual information that could incriminate each other. In 2025, The Daily Beast claimed Epstein remained a member at Mar-a-Lago for years after Trump claimed to have canceled his membership. In December 2025, Woody Allen stated he was "not sorry" about his friendship with Epstein, acknowledging they were neighbors by 2010. Allen stated in 2025 that none of the girlfriends Epstein had when they were neighbors were underage and described Epstein as "charming and personable." In a 2016 letter, Allen acknowledged knowing that several young women visited Epstein and that parties at his New York home included politicians, scientists, teachers, magicians, comedians, intellectuals, journalists, an entymologist, and a concert pianist, and noted Epstein’s townhome reminded him of Castle Dracula with young female vampires. In 2025, files released by the House Oversight Committee revealed that Noam Chomsky had closely befriended Epstein after his 2008 conviction, remaining in touch until at least 2017, including a formal letter of endorsement from 2017 or later in which he called Epstein a "highly valued friend and regular source of intellectual exchange and stimulation." A photo of Chomsky with Steve Bannon from Epstein’s estate and another showing him with Epstein on a flight in Epstein’s jet were released in December 2025. Prior to the release, Chomsky said he received around $270,000 from an account connected to Epstein while managing funds after his wife Carol’s death. Chomsky noted Epstein assisted his second wife Valeria in efforts to introduce him to jazz, though with "limited success." Hyoid bone breaks are more common in homicide by strangulation than in hangings; a 2010 study found them in 25% of hangings, while a 2010–2016 study found them in only 6% of cases. Hyoid breaks become more common with age due to bone brittleness. Forensic pathologist Cyril Wecht noted that hanging by leaning forward would not result in broken cervical bones.
